title: ST-HHOL: Spatio-Temporal Hierarchical Hypergraph Online Learning for Crime Prediction
one_liner: Predict where crime will happen next by capturing hidden patterns in sparse crime records, adjusting constantly as the world changes.
lead: Crime happens in cities where multiple factors (weather, events, foot traffic, past crimes) collide in space and time. Ordinary crime prediction looks at each location separately, or links them only as neighbors on a map. But real crime patterns are stranger: nearby crimes can reinforce each other, old patterns fade as neighborhoods change, and sparse records hide the true shapes of risk. This paper builds a machine that sees high-order crime patterns (clusters of related events that don't follow a simple neighbor map), tracks how those patterns shift over time, and retrains itself constantly to handle a non-stationary world (where old patterns stop working and new ones emerge).

problem.h2: Crime records are sparse and patterns are hidden
paras: Police data gives isolated crime reports—a theft here, a robbery there. To predict where crime will strike next, a machine needs to see which events reinforce each other (a robbery and a nearby theft within hours might signal a coordinated crime wave), which patterns matter more than others, and how neighborhoods change over months so old forecasts no longer hold. Ordinary time-series models assume the rules stay fixed. They also assume each location is nearly independent, or link locations only through a simple grid (a crime at corner A influences its four neighbors on the map grid). Neither assumption matches reality. Crime also depends on events we record: a concert draws crowds; a police blitz deters offenders. These contextual threads wrap around the neighborhoods in tangled ways—not as a regular grid.

A beginner might first try: throw all the sparse records into a standard prediction model with local neighborhoods. This fails because it misses the high-order patterns (which clusters of crimes tend to co-occur even if they are not adjacent on the map). As neighborhoods evolve, the model will go stale and predict confidently wrong events.

callout.html: ST-HHOL binds sparse crime data with contextual factors through a multi-level hypergraph (capturing hidden co-occurrence patterns), then retrains itself constantly to handle concept drift (when patterns shift and old rules break).

steps.text: Collect reported crimes (location, time, type) and contextual threads (events, foot traffic, weather) for each area.
Link crimes and neighborhoods not just by map proximity but by hidden co-occurrence: crimes that tend to cluster together over time, regardless of distance.
Each crime record and context thread flow through the graph layers; at each level, the model counts how strongly crimes reinforce or suppress each other.
After each new crime report arrives, fine-tune the model lightly to capture this week's pattern shifts without forgetting older seasonal trends.
Monthly or seasonally, retrain the full model to absorb structural changes (new neighborhoods, permanent police strategies).

paras: The paper changes how the model links crime events together. Instead of assuming each location is nearly isolated or connected only to map-grid neighbors, it builds a hypergraph: a graph where each edge can bind many nodes at once, and edges are arranged in layers (a hierarchy). A standard graph-edge joins two nodes (e.g., a map edge between two neighboring blocks); a hypergraph-edge can bind five crimes from scattered neighborhoods that tend to co-occur. The hierarchical layers let the model reason from local details (individual crime types and blocks) up to city-wide patterns (seasonal crime waves) and back down (specific predictions for block X at time Y).

hidden.name: Concept drift: how much the prediction rules are changing
paras: In ordinary machine learning, the model learns a fixed rule from data and then applies it forever. In crime prediction, the rule shifts. A police crackdown temporarily suppresses robbery; a new neighborhood opens and patterns flood in; seasons change the foot traffic that triggers petty theft. Concept drift is the measure of how much the true prediction rule is changing over time. The paper does not name a single 'importance' or 'influence' score; instead, it monitors two signals: (1) short-term prediction error (how far off the model's forecast is day-to-day—rising error signals a local pattern shift that needs a quick fine-tune), and (2) model-parameter stability (how much the learned weights are drifting from their last full-retraining—large drift signals that the model is slowly becoming obsolete and needs a seasonal retrain).

The paper's online-learning strategy uses these signals implicitly: if the daily error spikes, fine-tune immediately (short-term fix). If parameters have drifted steadily over weeks, call a full retrain (structural reset). This keeps the model responsive to weekly shifts and also anchored to seasonal truth.

heat.caption: Darker cells show drifting model parameters (weights shifting from their last reset); true spikes (w3, w9, w11) trigger immediate fine-tuning or retraining.

reads.html: Concept drift is the fact that the real world's rules are changing. Think of it like weather forecasting: rules that work in winter fail in summer. The model must notice when its predictions are going wrong and update itself.

ST-HHOL monitors daily prediction residuals (error size) and model-weight shifts across iterations, triggering short-term fine-tuning when error spikes or periodic full retraining when drift accumulates over weeks.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: from patterns to predictions to adaptation
paras: The paper's core insight is that crime patterns hide in co-occurrence relationships that a simple map grid cannot capture. A hypergraph is a tool for this: imagine each crime type at each location is a node, and edges bind nodes together. A normal edge joins two nodes (like a map-neighbor edge). A hypergraph edge can join many nodes at once—say, 'robberies, car thefts, and police responses in neighborhoods A, B, C, D tend to co-occur in waves.' This multi-way binding captures the hidden patterns sparse records conceal. The hierarchical structure lets the model reason up and down: at the bottom level, individual crime micro-events; at the top, city-wide seasonal crime climate; in the middle, neighborhood-cluster dynamics. Information flows up (aggregating local clues into broad patterns) and down (letting broad patterns shape local predictions).

But a static graph model, run once on old data, will eventually fail because the world changes. The paper adds online learning: as each new crime report arrives, the model's learned weights (the parameters that tell it which hypergraph edges matter most) can shift slightly in a quick fine-tune step. This catches daily fluctuations. But if the model fine-tunes every day without bound, it forgets seasonal structure. So the paper also does periodic retraining: every month or season, it resets and relearns from scratch (or mostly from scratch) using all recent data. This retraining erases the accumulated daily fine-tunings and rebuilds the stable long-term patterns.

Finally, the paper layers in a partially-frozen large-language model. A large-language model is trained on vast text data and learns abstract sequence patterns (e.g., 'Friday night often precedes theft-spike days'). By freezing most of its weights (keeping them fixed) and adapting only the attention mechanisms (the parts that decide which learned patterns to focus on for this prediction task), the model can use that abstract knowledge without overfitting to sparse crime data. It acts as an inductive bias: a nudge toward predicting plausible temporal patterns.

stages.s: Sparse crime records + context (weather, events, foot traffic)
Build hypergraph: link crimes that co-occur, even if distant
Hierarchical reasoning: aggregate upward to patterns, guide downward to location-time predictions
Online fine-tune: after each new report, nudge weights to match today's pattern
Periodic retraining: monthly, reset and rebuild to erase drift, lock in structural changes
Forecast: crime risk for each location at each hour in the next week

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Day 1: Model predicts 5 crimes at location X; 7 actually occur. Prediction error = (7-5)^2 = 4.

Last full retrain was 20 days ago; hypergraph edge for 'robbery co-occurrence' has drifted from 0.8 to 0.85, a shift of 0.05. Drift penalty = alpha × (0.85 - 0.8)^2 = 0.5 × 0.05^2 = 0.5 × 0.0025 = 0.00125 (tiny).

Total loss on day 1 = 4 + 0.00125 ≈ 4.00. The model fine-tunes to reduce this, nudging weights by small steps. Drift penalty keeps the nudges small, preserving the seasonal structure learned 20 days ago.

After 30 days, drift accumulates (many small nudges). A full retrain resets theta_i to new values fit to the past month, and theta_i_last_retrain jumps to match. Drift penalty drops to zero again, giving fine-tuning freedom for the next cycle.

math.note: The equation balances two goals: predict today's crimes correctly (first term), but without wandering so far from last month's structure that seasonal patterns break (second term).

charts.title: Static model (trained once, never updated)
charts.note: Accuracy drops as the real world's patterns drift away from the model's learned rules. By month 3, the model is nearly useless.

charts.title: This paper (online learning + retraining)
charts.note: Daily fine-tuning catches short-term shifts; monthly retraining locks in structural changes. Accuracy stays high, even as the world evolves.

items.html: If the model fine-tunes every single day without periodic retraining, it will forget long-term seasonal patterns (e.g., holiday crime changes). Then in December, it predicts January's rule. The paper's solution: periodic full retrain.

If the hypergraph binds every crime to every other crime (a dense fully-connected hypergraph), computing the forward pass becomes impossible. The paper must prune: only bind crimes that genuinely co-occur above a threshold. Too loose a threshold: it works; too tight: it misses the hidden patterns it was built to find.

items.b: Sparse data vanishes; hypergraph has no signal.
items.html: In neighborhoods with very few crime records, the hierarchical hypergraph has little evidence to work with. The model must learn from nearby neighborhoods (transfer) or lean heavily on the language-model's built-in knowledge of temporal patterns. If neither works, predictions become noise.

Tune the alpha (drift-penalty strength) so that fine-tuning adapts to real change without chasing noise. Schedule retraining at a seasonal boundary (not arbitrary). Start the hypergraph with a threshold that captures true co-occurrence, then validate on held-out weeks.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small synthetic crime city (10 neighborhoods, 365 days, 500 sparse crime reports). Define a true crime-generation rule that drifts: a police blitz at day 100 suppresses robbery (fewer patrols resources mean less robbery, because criminals avoid detected locations), and a new night-life zone at day 200 boosts theft (more nightlife crowds and alcohol mean more unguarded wallets, because more targets and reduced vigilance appear). Train a static model, a naive online-learning model (fine-tune every day with no retraining), and ST-HHOL (fine-tune + periodic retrain). Plot each model's prediction accuracy over time. The static model should degrade visibly after day 100 and day 200 (it learned the old rule and cannot adapt). The naive online-learner should fit the new patterns but then lose the old seasonal signal (it keeps shifting every day and forgets winter's slower-crime pattern). ST-HHOL should track the drifting rule and stay accurate across all seasons and interventions (quick fine-tune adapts, periodic retrain anchors).
demo.metric_eq: drift_robustness = min(accuracy_after_day_200) - min(accuracy_static_model); higher is better (ST-HHOL > 30%, static < 10%)
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss that online retraining is not optional: without periodic resets, even adaptive models slowly forget, and without fine-tuning, rigid models break the moment the world changes.
